newsitem.title: UK: UK investment watchdog due to sanction MGAM soon.
newsitem.headline: UK investment watchdog due to sanction MGAM soon.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG is counting the multi-million pound cost of last year's problems at its British fund arm, which should soon hear its fate at the hands of Britain's investments watchdog IMRO.
The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation is expected to complete the first stage of its probe into what went wrong at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management early next month.
"We are working towards an early finish to the case as soon as possible after the end of March," an IMRO spokeswoman told Reuters on Wednesday.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's sanction for control failures at MGAM is tipped to be the harshest ever meted out by IMRO, with a fine in excess of a million pounds ($1.6 million) expected.
Trading in three MGAM funds was suspended in September following the discovery of irregularities in valuations of unlisted securities in some of the unit trusts.

DMG is the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank. Deutsche's chief executive Hilmar Kopper said on Wednesday that the total cost of the problems at its British fund unit would be 1.1 to 1.2 billion marks (around $700 million or some 430 million pounds).
In December Deutsche agreed to a record compensation package of around 200 million pounds to retail investors. Compensation is due to be paid to investors by the end of April.

MGAM fund manager Peter Young was sacked by the firm and he is under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO). Young has said he is not guilty of any criminal activity and that he is being made a scapegoat for internal failings.
In addition to fining MGAM units, IMRO can impose other disciplinary actions when it completes its investigations.

Having brought the question of compensation to a hasty conclusion, IMRO will concentrate on internal corporate failings at Morgan Grenfell International Funds Management and Morgan Grenfell Unit Trust Managers -- the two firms it regulates -- rather than individuals when it concludes the first stage of its report.
IMRO's armoury includes being able to fine firms it regulates as much as it deems fit, banning them by revoking their licence, or possibly limiting the scope of their activities.
The largest fine IMRO has imposed to date was 750,000 pounds which it levied on fund management group Invesco.

The Young affair has already led to high-level casualties at MGAM with a purge in October of senior management, including chief executive Keith Percy and three other directors, after an internal probe revealed "management failings".

Deutsche also stepped in with a 180 million pound cash injection to buy out the suspect securities and ensure the funds could resume trading last September. This may not necessarily be written off in its entirety as it may have been able to realise some return from the stocks.

Other costs Deutsche will have to bear will include IMRO's expenses in bringing the case, the bills run up by both IMRO's and Deutsche's accounting and legal advisers, and the additional bureaucratic expenses of assessing individual losses and then making payments to a possible total of 90,000 retail investors.

Deutsche promised throughout to make good any losses to investors in the Morgan Grenfell European Growth Trust, the Morgan Grenfell Europa Fund and the Morgan Grenfell European Capital Growth Fund, two of which were managed by Young.

All investors in these funds at any time between August 1 1995 and September 5 1996 are being considered for compensation, which will be "the difference between the investment return from the fund and the return provided by a specially compiled index of comparable funds".
